Analysis of the PKGBUILD for safety of running makepkg --printsrcinfo.

The top-level/global scope of the PKGBUILD contains only standard variable assignments and source-array definitions. There are no top-level command substitutions, eval, curl, base64, or any other constructs that would execute code during sourcing. The functions (prepare(), build(), check(), package()) contain the build/test/install logic, but per the scope of this gate, these are not executed by makepkg --printsrcinfo.

The source array uses a VCS git source with a #tag= refspec, which is normal for a -git/versioned package. The checksum is populated (not SKIP), and there are no suspicious network operations at the global scope. No malicious or dangerous code is present in the top-level scope that would execute during this command.

The `.nvchecker.toml` file is a configuration file for **nvchecker**, a tool used by AUR maintainers to track upstream package versions. It is not a packaging script and executes nothing on its own. The file simply declares that the `rusthound-ce` package should check the upstream GitHub repository `g0h4n/RustHound-CE` for new releases tagged with the "v" prefix, using the latest release. This is a standard maintainer convenience file with no execution capability — it contains no network calls, no downloads, no `eval`, no base64, and no system modifications. There are no red flags: no obfuscation, no exfiltration, no backdoors. This is purely a version-notification configuration, a common and legitimate part of AUR package maintenance hygiene.

The source is explicitly referenced from the project's official GitHub repository (https://github.com/g0h4n/rusthound-ce) using a pinned version tag (v$pkgver), which is appropriate and expected behavior. The build process uses standard Cargo commands (cargo fetch, cargo build, cargo test) with the --frozen flag to prevent dependency modifications and ensure reproducibility. All functions (prepare, build, check, package) perform expected operations: fetching dependencies, compiling the application, running tests, and installing the binary and license files. No suspicious network operations, obfuscated code, or unexpected system modifications are present. The maintainer information and project URL appear legitimate for the BloodHound CE collector tool.
